claims.text: The initial HEA is fully single-phase.
The initial HEA has a homogeneous solute distribution.
The initial HEA has a fine-grained microstructure.
The untreated HEA has high toughness and ductility.
Elevated-temperature aging increases atomic mobility and local diffusion of minor solutes.
The increased mobility causes minor solutes to segregate to grain boundaries.
Segregated solutes nucleate fine intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries.
The grain-boundary intermetallic precipitates reduce grain-boundary cohesion.
The selected treatment can induce segregation and precipitation without extensive grain growth.
The treated material retains a refined grain structure.
The overall single-phase structure remains largely unaltered after treatment.
Treated samples will have lower fracture energy than untreated samples.
Treated samples will have lower ductility than untreated samples.
The precipitate-driven mechanism differs from conventional-alloy embrittlement, in which grain coarsening is prominent.
Very high temperatures may prevent or mask the proposed precipitate-driven embrittlement response.
Very rapid loading may prevent or mask the proposed precipitate-driven embrittlement response.
The magnitude of toughness reduction may vary with alloy composition and treatment parameters.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts a distinct intermetallic precipitate phase at grain boundaries while also saying that the overall structure remains single-phase. The matrix could remain single-phase, but the precipitate-containing material as a whole would not.

The hypothesis labels the mechanism as different from conventional-alloy embrittlement, yet its stated causal mechanism is grain-boundary solute segregation followed by brittle grain-boundary precipitation, the conventional mechanism identified in the task. The proposed distinction is instead based on limited grain growth, while the predicted-outcome field characterizes conventional embrittlement as grain-coarsening-driven.
